name: 8-bit
means: Sprite-era pixel art: a coarse visible grid where every pixel is a deliberately placed square, a palette of a dozen or so colours, no anti-aliasing anywhere, gradients faked with ordered dithering, and each form outlined in a darker shade of its own fill.
prose: 8-bit pixel art sprite work, a coarse visible grid of large square pixels with hard aliased edges and no smoothing anywhere, a strict twelve-colour palette, shading done with ordered checkerboard dithering rather than blending, each form outlined in a darker tone of its own colour, flat black background
negative_add: smooth, anti-aliased, photorealistic, 3d render, gradient, fine detail
works_for: No, and not for the usual reason. Even if LTX-2.3 held the texture, i2v produces smooth sub-pixel motion, and sub-pixel motion is a contradiction in a style whose entire premise is that the pixel is the smallest unit. You get a pixel-art image being smoothly warped, which is exactly what it is. INFERRED, not measured.
note: WEAK ON BOTH ENGINES - the clearest mark-it-unavailable case in this set. Diffusion at 1344x768 cannot hold a pixel grid: what comes back is pixel-art-FLAVOURED, with inconsistent cell sizes, anti-aliased edges inside cells, and three hundred colours where you asked for twelve. It reads as a photograph of pixel art rather than as pixel art. REACH FOR THIS INSTEAD: render whatever you actually want at normal resolution using flat_vector, then do the pixelation in the deterministic tier where it is exact - nearest-neighbour downscale to sprite resolution, palette quantise, nearest-neighbour scale back up. A handful of ffmpeg arguments, CORRECT by construction rather than approximately obeyed, which is the same case studio/looks/ makes for grading. animagine knows the danbooru tag 'pixel art' and returns the same mush, so the anime path is no rescue and the tags field is left empty.
verdict: Genuine chunky pixel quantisation. Works on qwen; inert on the illustration engine.
